newsitem.title: USA: Decision on U.S. pilot's discharge bid expected.
newsitem.headline: Decision on U.S. pilot's discharge bid expected.

text.p: The first woman B-52 bomber pilot waited on Thursday for an Air Force decision on whether it will grant her an honourable discharge or proceed with a court-martial against her on charges of adultery and lying.
But despite heavy media speculation that the announcement would come Thursday, there was no official word on when the Air Force would make known its plans for Lt. Kelly Flinn.

Flinn, who is 26 and single, has asked the Air Force to allow her to resign with an honourable discharge in lieu of being court-martialed on charges that she committed adultery, lied during an official investigation and disobeyed a direct order.
Flinn's court martial was put on hold on Monday to give Air Force Secretary Sheila Widnall time to consider her request.
While lawmakers in Washington have come out in support of Flinn, signs emerged on Wednesday indicating the Air Force may not give her an honourable discharge.

In testimony before Congress, Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Ronald Fogleman said the dispute over Flinn was more serious than the issue of adultery. Responding to questions from Iowa Sen. Harkin, Fogelman said Flinn was an officer entrusted to fly planes carrying nuclear weapons, but that she had misled superiors and disobeyed orders.
"It makes us look ridiculous because people don't know the facts," Fogleman said. "What we are doing in the Air Force is not trying to regulate the sexual mores of America."
Harkin had attacked the Air Force, accusing officials of wasting money chasing down cases of adultery.
"I think the Air Force is looking ridiculous on this," Harkin said. He suggested he might try to add a provision to the Air Force annual spending bill to address the issue.
Other lawmakers stepped up pressure on the Air Force to drop the charges and grant Flinn her resignation request.

"Allow her to leave the military with dignity," said Representative Nita Lowey, a New York Democrat and one of several Congresswoman who came out in support of Flinn at a news conference on Wednesday.

"Kelly Flinn is not innocent -- but neither is the Air Force," Lowey said. "This case has been bungled from the very beginning. The Air Force should have offered Kelly Flinn counselling, warnings, and a transfer. Instead it has thrown the book at her, treating her like a criminal."
Air Force Secretary Sheila Widnall had no comment on the Flinn case after testifying before a Senate Appropriations subcommittee, which was discussing next year's Air Force budget.

Widnall could offer Flinn an honourable, general or dishonourable discharge or she could reject the request entirely. Flinn has said she will only accept an honourable discharge, and will take her chances with a court-martial if she is offered anything less.
Flinn, wearing a brown leather bomber jacket over her olive green flight suit, told reporters on Wednesday she had received hundreds of letters of support.
The charges against Flinn have sparked a vocal public debate, and her defendants have argued that she is being unfairly persecuted for something that is commonplace in civilian life.
Flinn has admitted she had an affair with a married civilian, but said he told her he had legally separated from his wife. She is also charged with having an affair with an enlisted man.
